The Enlightenment. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, an intellectual and cultural movement swept Europe and North America that elevated reason, empirical science, and individual rights as the basis for knowledge, morality, and political legitimacy. Enlightenment thinkers rejected the authority of tradition, religious dogma, and monarchy in favor of rationalism, the scientific method, religious tolerance, and democratic governance.

The movement emerged from seventeenth-century developments in science and philosophy. Isaac Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation demonstrated that nature operated by mathematical principles rather than mystical forces, providing a model for rational understanding. John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding established empiricism as the epistemological foundation for scientific inquiry, arguing that all knowledge derives from sensory experience, not innate ideas. René Descartes championed reason as the primary tool for discovering truth, influencing nearly every major Enlightenment thinker.

In political philosophy, John Locke articulated the theory of natural rights, that humans are born with inalienable rights to life, liberty, and property, and that legitimate government requires the consent of the governed, foundational to liberal democracy. Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that legitimate sovereignty belongs to the general will of the people, asserting that people, not monarchs, are the true source of political authority. Montesquieu advocated the separation of powers, dividing government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches to prevent tyranny.

Enlightenment thinkers applied reason to nearly every domain. David Hume rigorously analyzed morality and causation. Adam Smith created the framework for modern economics. Immanuel Kant systematized reason itself. The deism favored by many offered a middle ground between atheism and dogmatic Christianity, dismantling arguments for religious authority over thought.

Thinkers challenged the divine right of monarchy, arguing that rulers derive power from the people and remain subject to reason and natural law. This critique of authority elevated individual reason as the judge of truth, fundamentally shifting legitimacy from tradition to rational argument. The salon culture of Paris and other European cities became spaces where educated men and women debated philosophy, science, and politics, democratizing intellectual life. Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert's vast Encyclopédie spread reason and empirical understanding across Europe.

The Enlightenment's legacy includes both triumphs and shadows. Its insistence that reason, not tradition or revelation, is the arbiter of truth altered Western thought fundamentally. The scientific method it established remains the foundation of modern science. Its political philosophy became the intellectual basis for the United States Constitution, the Declaration of the Rights of Man during the French Revolution, and liberal democracy itself. Yet this same rationalist certainty would later guide twentieth-century totalitarianisms. Still, the movement created the concept of the public intellectual and the public sphere of rational debate that, at its best, defines democratic discourse.
